World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Farmer rescues kangaroo from muddy dam amid 'perilous' drought conditions
World.content:
A farmer has pulled a bogged kangaroo from a dry dam as landholders and wildlife carers sound the alarm over drought conditions in western New South Wales.

Photos capture the kangaroo moments before he was rescued from the dam near Narromine in the state's Central West.

The animal became bogged in the sticky black silt while searching for water in an increasingly barren landscape.

The land is dry and water is scarce in Central West NSW. (Supplied: Scott Richardson)

The farmer who found the animal said conditions had deteriorated rapidly.

"We're in a big rain deficit at the moment. We haven't had any substantial rain since September," farmer Scott Richardson said.

"The dams are dry. They didn't catch any water in that event, and they've certainly caught nothing since.

"Things are rather perilous."

Rescue's happy ending

The Narromine grazier said he was relieved his kangaroo encounter had a happy ending.

"When I drove past and saw him stuck in the dam I thought there'd only be one option: to humanely euthanise him," Mr Richardson said.

"Then, I saw he still had some strength left and had put up a fight. He'd crawled a good 15 metres through the thick, swampy mud.

Scott Richardson is relieved his kangaroo rescue ended happily. (Supplied: Scott Richardson)

"His face had dropped down into the mud. I managed to get him out in time because he'd probably been in the dam for a good day or so. He was relatively light.

"I thought I was going to get towelled up a bit trying to help, but he was as happy to hop away as I was to see it."

The farmer said it was important for everyone to "show some humility" during this tough period.

"When wildlife and birds are doing it tough, trying to find water to drink, a little bit of compassion is always good to have," he said.

"Farmers are the stewards of the land. We do give a toss, and we do care."

The kangaroo had dragged itself through the sticky mud, where it became stuck. (Supplied: Scott Richardson)

Wildlife carers 'overwhelmed'

Volunteer Tanya O'Donohue, from Warrumbungle Wildlife Rescue & Rehabilitation, said dry conditions had escalated at an alarming pace.

"This drought went from zero to 100 in the last six to eight weeks," she said.

"In the [later stages] of the last drought, I noticed animals becoming skeletal. But I'm already seeing that now.

"Animals are really struggling. They're terribly emaciated.

"It's overwhelming because you can't save them all."

Tanya O'Donohue is retiring after dedicating more than 30 years of to saving injured animals. (Supplied)

Ms O'Donohue said she was already overwhelmed with rescues and requests to humanely euthanase injured wildlife.

"Everything is drought-affected. When I drive around, I'm seeing nocturnal animals out during daylight hours looking for food, kangaroos in paddocks that are devoid of feed or taking risks coming into towns and up next to roads," she said.

"Even spring-fed dams around my area are starting to dry up."

For volunteer carers, the emotional and financial toll is relentless, with Ms O'Donohue travelling hundreds of kilometres across the Central West for rescues.

"I have to fill up a diesel vehicle to travel hundreds of kilometres to do a rescue. Even for a euthanasia, I'm looking at over 100 kilometres," Ms O'Donohue said.

Coonabarabran is two hours north-west of the Narromine kangaroo rescue, but the landscape is also looking barren. (Supplied: Tanya O'Donohue)

She recently announced her retirement from her all-consuming carer role due to health reasons.

"I've been doing this for 33 years. I'm tired. I do a lot of rescues," Ms O'Donohue.

"My retirement couldn't come at a worse time, but I know I can't do another drought physically."

She said she was "praying" others would step up.

"I'm hoping it gives other carers an opportunity to take the reins. I'll help in other ways," she said.

Droughts damage the species

Ms O'Donohue said breeding had largely halted; a natural response during dry times that highlighted the harsh conditions.

"The female kangaroos I'm pulling off the road have no pouch young, which tells me how bad it is — it's extreme," she said.

"I believe we're having a kangaroo population crash. Another year and there'll be millions of animals dead through New South Wales alone."

This skinny kangaroo had a lucky escape from the dry dam. (Supplied: Scott Richardson)

The animal rescuer said more compassion was needed for an animal that was often treated like a pest.

"Kangaroos are the most misunderstood species," she said.

"Koalas were a common species once, and the same thing will happen to kangaroos eventually. Humans put them under so much pressure with shooting and loss of habitat."

"We've got to learn to co-exist with our wildlife, otherwise there'll be nothing left."

World.title: Josh Hazlewood crushes Capitals in IPL bowling clinic
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has delivered another bowling masterpiece in the IPL, his four-wicket burst in tandem with Indian star Bhuvneshwar Kumar blowing away the flimsy challenge of Delhi Capitals for champions, Royal Challengers Bengaluru.

The veteran Australian Test star, who's been flying since his return from injury two-and-a-half weeks ago, blasted through Delhi's top-order, taking two wickets with his first two balls and a third in his following over in Monday's clash.

With Kumar also taking three wickets in his opening two overs after RCB had asked Delhi to bat, the pair left the Capitals reeling at an extraordinary 6-8, looking in danger of recording the lowest IPL total ever (RCB's 49 against Kolkata in 2017).

Only resistance from Abishek Porel (30) and David Miller (19) enabled Delhi to avoid that fate as they limped to 75, but in the 17th over, Hazlewood returned ruthlessly to finish the job, yorking Porel for his best IPL figures of 4-12 off 3.3 overs.

Kumar was just as good, taking 3-5 off his three as the pair left Delhi 6-13 at the end of the first six powerplay overs with their irresistible mix of swing, seam and the occasional hostile short one.

But once RCB had cruised to 1-77 for a nine-wicket win in 6.3 overs, with Virat Kohli (23no) becoming the first man to pass 9,000 IPL runs — no-one else has even gone past 8,000 — Hazlewood was judged to have edged it as player of the match.

He got danger man KL Rahul, fresh from scoring 152 not out in his last knock, with his short, sharp first ball that climbed on the Indian Test batter and forced him to rush his pull shot, so he steepled it up for a simple catch to wicketkeeper Jitesh Sharma.

Next ball, he had Sameer Rizvi caught behind, and in his following over, served up a vicious, rearing snorter that looped up off Nitish Rana's gloves.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Those guys are so good with the new ball," said teammate Devdutt Padikkal, who eased RCB to the winning line alongside Kohli with 34 not out off 13 balls.

"In the slips, I'm expecting a catch every ball, and that's not something you'd say in a T20, but when those two are bowling, every ball is an opportunity."

Hazlewood loved every minute of this rare bowler's day in the IPL sun.

"Probably turning up here after 500-plus runs in the last game, you don't expect that," he said.

He only had one regret. That he wasn't allowed to bowl a fourth-straight over after his sensational first 18 balls.

"It would have been nice to bowl four-straight and get off the field," he said.

AAP

World.title: Community divided over $1.5bn waste-to-energy incinerator proposal
World.content:
A proposed $1.5 billion waste-to-energy incinerator has split a southern Queensland community, with supporters arguing it will ease Queensland's growing landfill crisis and opponents fearing health risks.

Waste company Cleanaway has put forward plans for the Bromelton Energy and Resource Centre just outside of Beaudesert on the Scenic Rim, about 70km south of Brisbane.

If approved, the facility would process 760,000 tonnes of waste each year.

According to Cleanaway, that would divert about 12 per cent of Queensland's waste from landfill and generate enough electricity to power 105,000 homes and businesses.

The incinerator would burn rubbish at temperatures of about 850 degrees. (Supplied: Cleanaway)

The plant works by burning waste to heat a boiler which creates steam that drives a turbine and generates electricity.

Waste-to-energy plants already operate in Western Australia, while proposals are also being considered in Parkes in New South Wales and on the Gold Coast.

But while supporters say the Scenic Rim proposal could bring jobs and investment to the region, some residents say they do not want the state's waste problem brought to their doorstep.

Health concerns

Lizz Hills is a member of Keep the Scenic Rim Scenic, a community group that initially formed to oppose coal seam gas expansion in the area in the 2010s, and has reformed to oppose the waste incinerator proposal.

She said she joined Cleanaway's community advisory group with an open mind before deciding she was against the project — predominantly for health and environmental reasons.

Lizz Hills is part of the Keep the Scenic Rim Scenic group. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

She said she feared pollutants coming out of the flue — and was concerned as the technology had been prohibited in parts of New South Wales, including Sydney and the Australian Capital Territory.

"I don't want them anywhere near my family. I don't want them anywhere near our schools, my community," she said.

"If we've got two major capital cities going 'let's not put incinerators here', why would we accept one in the Scenic Rim?

" Are we just outsourcing a city's waste problem to regional Australia? "

Keep the Scenic Rim Scenic was initially established to oppose coal seam gas expansion in the area in the 2010s. It has reformed to oppose the incinerator. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

A 'safe alternative to landfill'

Cleanaway said the facility would use combustion controls, flue-gas treatment and continuous monitoring to keep emissions below environmental standards.

The company said 99.9 per cent of emissions from the facility's flue stack would consist of gases already present in the atmosphere.

These include nitrogen and oxygen, along with carbon dioxide — which will make up about nine per cent of the emissions.

The rubbish will burn at about 850 degrees, which Cleanaway said would remove harmful compounds — while multiple flue gas treatment processes will remove pollutants.

About 0.1 per cent of the emissions will be compounds that need to be monitored to ensure they don't exceed human health safety limits.

"The BERC is not an incinerator like we have come to know them from decades past," Cleanaway said.

"This technology is always improving and thousands of modern energy from waste facilities around the world prove that this is a safe alternative to landfill.

" At BERC, we will use the latest technology to control pollution, meet the strict environmental standards and protect the health of all. "

The company said it would make emissions monitoring data public and would shut the facility down if necessary, in response to any incident.

Experts divided on health impacts

Dr Peter Tait from the Australian Public Health Association said older generations of incinerators had been linked to cancers and birth defects.

"With newer incinerators, the claim is that they have technology to remove a lot of the bad stuff out of the emissions that are coming out of the smokestack," he said.

" Work we did more recently shows … the incinerators haven't been in operation for long enough for health impacts to appear, and so it's too early to be able to make the claim that they have no impacts or minimal impacts. "

Dr Peter Tait says he is sceptical of health claims made about new generation waste incinerators. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Dr Tait said any future facility would need close monitoring, particularly during startup and shutdown periods, when the risk of exposure could increase.

But Professor Damien Batstone from the University of Queensland's Australian Centre for Water and Environmental Biotechnology said recent reviews of modern waste-to-energy technology had found no evidence linking facilities to cancer.

He said new plants were far more advanced than earlier generations.

"We're now in generation four or five of waste incinerator technology, so gaseous management is very effective now," he said.

"You've got things like dioxins, heavy metals, polyaromatic hydrocarbons and a number of other contaminants like PFAS that need to be removed.

" Current technologies remove those very effectively. "

Damien Batstone says incinerators are only a medium term solution to the waste issue. (ABC News)

Incinerators 'medium-term measure'

Professor Batstone said waste-to-energy should be seen as an interim measure while Australia moved towards a circular economy.

"[Landfill] is starting to run out," he said.

"We need better options to manage waste in the long term — that's where we're moving towards with society, but it'll take us a while to get there and we need something that can fill the gap."

He said while Australia was "on the way" to a circular economy — which refers to recovering and reusing all elements of a production cycle — the country was not there yet.

"Over the next 20 to 30 years, we will move in that direction," he said.

" But at the moment there is going to be a substantial stream which can't be recycled ... waste-to-energy offers another opportunity. "

He said the technology was expensive and warned any proposal would also need to manage issues such as truck movements and local pollution.

Thousands of new homes are expected to be built in Beaudesert in the coming years. (ABC News)

Incinerator's economic boost

Back in Beaudesert, local chamber of commerce president John Powell said he believed the project could help support the region's rapid growth.

"We've got 4,000 new homes coming here in the next 15 years, that's 20,000 extra people," he said.

" A waste-to-energy facility would allow more industry to come here and tap into lower cost electricity and would be just the tonic we need. "

Mr Powell said he hoped the Bromelton State Development Area, where the facility would be built, could eventually become a broader circular economy precinct, attracting recycling and manufacturing businesses.

He said he believed waste-to-energy incineration should only be used as a "last option" for material that could not be recycled.

Mr Powell said he had confidence government agencies would monitor the facility and ensure it met environmental standards.

Cleanaway submitted a planning application to the Office of the Coordinator-General in March. A decision is expected later this year or in early 2027.

World.title: Aussie rugby may benefit from copying NZ's lateral thinking approach
World.content:
One match is hardly a recommended sample size, but the risk the Crusaders took by starting Leicester Fainga'anuku at openside flanker paid off during Super Round.

Fainga'anuku, a 12-Test All Black more accustomed to playing in the centres or wing, was impressive in the Crusaders' 35-20 win over the NSW Waratahs in front of a sellout crowd at Christchurch's new stadium on Friday night.

The Crusaders deserve praise for "thinking outside the square", although it is not the first time a back has switched to the loose forwards at the professional level, with the Springboks' André Esterhuizen a prominent example.

The concept of "hybrid" players has been discussed locally, with Wallabies legend Matt Burke recently suggesting Reds winger Filipo Daugunu had the ability to play openside flanker.

Lateral thinking needs to be encouraged in Australian rugby, as innovative ideas have previously been successful.

A noted admirer of Edward de Bono's creative thinking strategies, former Wallabies coach Rod Macqueen orchestrated Stephen Larkham's switch from fullback/utility to fly half in 1998.

The following year, Larkham played a starring role in Australia's Rugby World Cup victory.

Stephen Larkham became one of the best fly halves in world rugby. (Getty Images/ALLSPORT: Darren England)

Given the Wallabies' current predicament in the fly half position, would adopting a similar approach work?

Maybe. Or maybe not.

But examining Australia's stocks of fullbacks, centres and scrum halves could be a worthwhile exercise to find the Wallabies' next great 10.

Taking a punt on positional switches has worked in rugby league.

Cameron Munster and Nicho Hynes are two shining examples of players in the contemporary game who started the NRL careers as fullbacks before successfully shifting to the halves.

McReight's decision to gamble

Queensland Reds captain Fraser McReight should not blame himself for his side's agonising 36-33 super-point loss to the Blues on Saturday night.

During extra time, McReight was penalised for entering a ruck from an offside position, allowing Beauden Barrett the opportunity to kick the winning goal from the tee.

McReight's indiscretion did provide the Blues with the decisive moment to ice their win.

Fraser McReight chanced his arm at the breakdown against the Blues. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

But the sixth-placed Reds had not helped their cause earlier in the match by twice putting themselves in a position — at 21-7 and 33-21 down — where they needed to chase the Blues on the scoreboard.

The decision to attack a defensive ruck is consistent with McReight's role as a jackal-style openside flanker.

They are gamblers who play on the edge at the risk of being penalised at the breakdown, yet their value to teams cannot be overstated.

McReight got pinged on this occasion, but his skill set has helped the Reds win many times.

Brumbies in a hole

Back in round two, there was every reason to believe the ACT Brumbies were a title contender when they disposed of the Crusaders 50-24 at their former home ground in Christchurch.

Teams do not defeat the Crusaders when playing across the Tasman in such a manner purely by chance.

But an inconsistent record at Canberra Stadium and a 45-12 thrashing dished out by the Hurricanes in Super Round have cast doubt on their credentials to lift the trophy at the end of the season.

Beating the Hurricanes in New Zealand was always going to be a tall order, but the Brumbies did not fire a shot on Saturday.

They were pushed around by the second-placed Hurricanes, who scored seven tries to two.

The Brumbies were outclassed by the Hurricanes in Super Round. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

With a 5-5 (win-loss) return, the Brumbies are fifth on the standings after 11 rounds, so their finals hopes are not in ruins.

But do they give their supporters confidence they can reach the play-offs with only four matches left in their regular-season campaign?

They play the Reds and Waratahs on the road, having lost to both teams in Canberra this season.

And with their 2-3 record at home, they cannot be considered overwhelming favourites to beat the Western Force and Moana Pasifika in their final two matches in the national capital.

Zac Lomax's encouraging performances have seemingly boosted the Force's morale, while Moana are showing no lack of fight in what is likely to be their last season in Super Rugby Pacific.

It is a massive month coming up for the Brumbies to prove they are worthy of playing finals.

Tahs fall but show effort

Prior to Super Round, the Waratahs' most-recent visit to New Zealand was not fondly remembered.

They were stood over by the Chiefs, who posted a dominant 42-14 victory in Hamilton almost a month ago.

The Waratahs could not get past the Crusaders in Christchurch. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

The Waratahs showed greater effort against the Crusaders on Friday night, although they let themselves down with poor discipline and turnovers.

Two players received yellow cards and they were on the end of a 13-7 penalty count.

Twice — in the space of five minutes in the second half — they wasted vital field position when they lost lineouts on their throw inside the Crusaders' 22.

The Waratahs only had 42 per cent of possession for the match, so they could ill-afford squandering ideal attacking platforms.

The visitors did produce some highlights though, such as Sid Harvey's first-half try after Jack Debreczeni found the young winger with a pinpoint cross-field kick.

Debreczeni's quick thinking exploited the condensed Crusaders' defensive line to help establish a short-lived 13-7 lead.

Using the Chiefs' loss as a measuring stick, it was an improved performance from the Waratahs, who remain an outside chance of making the finals in eighth place on the standings.

World.title: They were Port Arthur's first victims. Thirty years on, their legacy continues
World.content:
Sally and David Martin had long dreamed of restoring their rundown cottage on the Tasman Peninsula into a picturesque guesthouse.

Carly Martin's grandparents were the first victims of the Port Arthur massacre. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

When the Seascape bed and breakfast finally opened in the late 1980s, it became so popular it was usually booked out.

"It was so successful, [they] would have to put 'no vacancy' on the gate to get a day off," their granddaughter Carly Martin recalled.

Carly Martin looks at an old photo of the Seascape property. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Situated 3 kilometres up the highway from the historic penal colony of Port Arthur, Seascape attracted visitors from across the globe.

" My grandmother always used to say, 'I don't need to travel the world, the world comes to me.' "

Carly Martin's dad, Glen (left), with his parents, Sally and David Martin. (Supplied: Carly Martin)

On arrival, guests would be offered a selection of her grandmother's homemade treats, including relish and creamed corn.

"She would also provide a cup of tea and a homemade coconut biscuit and a bit of conversation for check-in," Ms Martin said.

It was such a special experience for guests that years later, letters would arrive in the Seascape mailbox from people reminiscing about their time there.

" [They] touched a lot of people's lives, and it must have meant something to [the guests] to stay with them. "

A 1989 newspaper story on the Seascape bed and breakfast. (Supplied: Carly Martin)

Grandparents never far from mind

But on April 28, 1996 — Ms Martin lost her grandparents.

A gunman, whom a judge later found "had long harboured a grudge" against the couple, had entered the Seascape property and murdered them.

Her grandparents were the first victims of what was to become the worst mass shooting in Australia's modern history.

"I think about them every single day," Ms Martin said.

Sally and David Martin. (Supplied: Carly Martin)

After leaving the Seascape property, the gunman drove to Port Arthur, where visitors were enjoying a day at the historic site.

About 1:30pm, the sound of gunfire ripped through the air.

In just 15 seconds, 12 people were fatally shot inside the Broad Arrow Cafe.

Less than 90 seconds later, another eight people were killed.

The shootings at the Port Arthur historic site happened at the cafe, the gift shop and in the car park. (Facebook: Port Arthur Historic Site/Dee Kramer/Above Down Under)

As the gunman made his way back to the Seascape cottage, he murdered 13 more people.

It was not until the following morning, after setting fire to the bed and breakfast, that he was arrested.

In total, 35 people were killed, almost two dozen were wounded and many more were psychologically scarred.

A memorial to the 35 people killed in the 1996 Port Arthur massacre exists on the former site of the Broad Arrow Cafe. (AAP: Robyn Grace)

Decades on, victims remembered

Today — on the 30th anniversary of the tragedy — a memorial service is being held in what remains of Port Arthur's old cafe, which has since been turned into a memorial garden.

It's a place where the name of the gunman, who was sentenced to life imprisonment with no parole, is not acknowledged.

The service, which has involved consultation with people impacted by the tragedy, will offer an opportunity to reflect on the enduring legacy of one of Australia's darkest days.

A memorial cross lists the names of the victims. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Walter Mikac's messages 30 years on from Port Arthur On April 28, 1996, a gunman killed 35 people at Port Arthur. Walter Mikac's wife and two daughters were among them. Thirty years on, he says gun control is as important as ever.

Some of the victims' relatives, including Ms Martin and her family, will be among those attending the memorial.

A survivor of the tragedy and a young member of the local community will speak at the service, and a song titled Always Remember will also be performed by local singers.

Then, at 1:30 pm — the same time when so many lives were cut short on April 28, 1996 — a minute's silence will be observed.

"Thirty years after the Port Arthur massacre, the terrible, indiscriminate cruelty of that day remains beyond understanding," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement.

"Australia pauses today to remember the 35 people whose lives and futures were so pitilessly stolen from them just because they happened to be there.

" We think of everyone whose world was shattered by the loss of those who had been the bright centre of their lives, their love left desperately wrapped around an absence. "

Mr Albanese said the gun controls that were enacted after the tragedy in 1996 were a testament to the "extraordinary courage that emerged from shattering grief".

"This is what we hold on to — the abiding memory that somehow amid the most terrible darkness the best of humanity found a way to shine," he said.

"Three decades on from that day when our nation stopped, let us stand together as we stood together then, united in love for everyone who never came home."

'It never goes away'

First responders who attended the unfolding emergency in 1996 will also be marking the anniversary.

"The events of that day changed many lives, and our thoughts are with those who continue to carry that loss, including emergency responders," Tasmania Police Commissioner Donna Adams said.

"As an emergency response agency, we will always remember.

"But we also recognise our resilience, and we remain focused on moving forward together with strength and hope."

Tasman mayor Rod Macdonald said the impact of the tragedy continues to resonate across the community.

"It's something you just learn to live with, but it never goes away, you never forget," he said.

Despite its enduring impact, he said people on the Tasman Peninsula had shown resilience in the 30 years since the tragedy.

"[There's a] very strong sense of community, [a] very connected community, and I think a welcoming community," he said.

"We rely on [the] visitor economy — it's a major part of our economic success and employment opportunities and all the jobs that go with the various industries [that] are critical to our region.

" And we want to continue that, build on what we have, to make it an even better place to live than it is. "

Seascape is still operating. (Supplied: Glen Martin)

'We kept going'

Three decades on, the Seascape cottage that burned down in 1996 is long gone.

But the Seascape sign is still attached to the brick wall at the front of the property.

And down the driveway, past trees that have grown tall over the past 30 years, Ms Martin's father Glen now resides in one of the two buildings that remain on site.

"[Port Arthur] is a place where there has been a lot of tragedy," Ms Martin said.

"But I think, speaking from a family perspective, Dad never wanted us to be defined by that.

" He didn't want us to become more victims of that massacre. "

Carly Martin says her family "didn't want it to ruin our lives". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

She said the anniversary was a chance to reflect on the legacy of her grandparents, including their devotion to making Seascape a special place.

"We got on with things, and we kept going," she said.

"We went back to work and we didn't want it to ruin our lives.

World.title: Two Marios behind a Melbourne institution celebrate its 40th birthday
World.content:
In the late 1990s, Melbourne institution Marios caused a firestorm when it denied comedian Jerry Seinfeld team's entreaties to secure a table for breakfast.

After all, there was a strict no-booking policy in place, which remains today, 40 years after the Fitzroy cafe first opened its doors.

However, that has not stopped many thousands of everyday diners — and celebrities from Kylie Minogue, to Ryan Gosling and Heath Ledger — filling the Fitzroy cafe's sought-after tables to enjoy brekkie, a coffee, a glass of wine or some classic Italian fare.

Many high-profile people, including Kylie Minogue, have visited Marios over the decades. (Supplied)

Today, Marios will celebrate its 40th by giving diners a free magazine-style publication celebrating its history, with contributions from an array of famous fans including Colin Hay, Sam Pang, Red Symons and Mary Coustas, each naming their favourite dish.

'Headquarters for alternative Melbourne'

Mario Maccarone says when he and Mario De Pasquale opened the cafe — and catering business out the back — in the city's now-iconic Brunswick Street, it was a very rundown area with cheap rent.





Mario Maccarone (right) and Mario De Pasquale outside the cafe in more recent times. (Supplied: Helga Salwe) "Brunswick Street was mostly boarded-up shops with students or artists living in the shopfronts or having studios in the shopfronts, or rehearsal rooms for bands," says Maccarone.

Or, as he also puts it, "the headquarters for alternative Melbourne".

He says it was a fantastic place to be, with PBS and Triple R community radio stations in the area, the Universal Theatre on Victoria Street, and the Last Laugh in Collingwood.

"And we were welcoming of all kinds of minorities, so we were embraced by everyone."

In the early days, all sorts of creative deals were cut by agents, promoters and managers using the cafe's one public payphone.

A hit from the start

Maccarone and De Pasquale, who'd met as waiters at Melbourne restaurant Tsindos, got the keys to the cafe, now a Melbourne institution, on Maccarone's 24th birthday.

De Pasquale, the senior of the pair by about eight years, had started his own catering business, which was taking off.

Maccarone, who helped him as a waiter, said they opened the cafe at the front almost as a bit of an afterthought — "and of course what happened was the cafe went crazy straight away".

In the early days, De Pasquale, a qualified cook, ran the kitchen while the younger Mario waited tables.

"But as time went by, it just made sense to have two Marios out the front," says Maccarone.



"That meant we could cover more hours, and there was always a Mario in the building."

A Marios float during a popular waiters' race event on Brunswick Street. (Supplied)

Maccarone says they wanted to provide an honest "eating house" that was a bistro, restaurant and cafe all rolled into one. But along with wholesome Italian fare, it also had a bit of flair about it.

There were proper tablecloths, and "waiters that looked like waiters", which he says was something of anomaly in 1980s Fitzroy.

However not everything was as slick as it could be; in the first year, the cafe only had one toilet, which diners could only access by walking through the kitchen.

Filling a gap in Melbourne's hospitality scene

Maccarone says he and De Pasquale had a feeling there were two main things missing in Melbourne hospitality.

An early menu from 1987, featuring the cafe's popular all-day breakfast. (Supplied)

One was all-day breakfast, in a time when even finding somewhere to go out for breakfast was tricky.

"If there were some breakfast places, they'd stopped serving breakfast at 10 in the morning, and most of our audience hasn't even gotten out of bed at that stage," he says.

"A lot of the artists and musicians in the area just love the fact they could come at one o'clock, two o'clock or three o'clock in the afternoon and have breakfast."

They also decided early on that as long as the doors were open, the kitchen wouldn't close. So at, say 5pm, you could have breakfast, lunch or dinner.

Loyal staff, customers stay for the long haul

Customer Timothy has been dining at Marios since he was a uni student in the early 1990s.

These days he still goes about three times each week, often with his wife and four kids, and likes the fact many of the staff have been around for years.

"Once you start going to a place for a long time, you get a family feel," he says.

Marios staff member Dan Barron out front at the Melbourne institution. (Supplied: Julian Kingma)

"Now my [older] daughter, who turned 18 just recently, she comes here with her girlfriends. It's intergenerational."

The Fitzroy North resident pinpoints the garlic bread, and the spaghetti bolognese as his hot favourites, and plans to join today's 40th celebrations.

Even if Marios isn't offering day one menu prices, like it did for its 30th anniversary.



"Fifty-cent coffees, and $1.50 pastas ... they should do that every day," Timothy laughs.

One retirement down, no plans for a second

About five years ago, the older Mario retired, but not before staying longer than intended to help their business survive the pandemic.

The two Marios pictured at work in the early 1990s. (Supplied)

During that time, the cafe also sold groceries and sent its waiters, waistcoats and all, to deliver meals to people's front doors, says Maccarone.

Along the way, Mario's has also continued its popular tradition of hosting a different art exhibition every three weeks.

Maccarone, whose daughter Milla now also works part-time at the cafe, has no plans to retire anytime soon, still thriving on the interactions he has with customers.

"I still love it. The place is successful, people love it — they tell me constantly," he says.

"So it's pretty easy to be proud of it, and pretty easy to enjoy it."

World.title: How a $2.2 trillion dream city in the Saudi desert got wound back
World.content:
The war in the Middle East is forcing one of the region's biggest players to rethink some of its grand plans, with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's trillion-dollar Vision 2030 rocked by the conflict.

The blueprint for Saudi Arabia's future, unveiled a decade ago, had outlined a glittering future for the kingdom as a hub for major events and sports to compete with its Gulf neighbours, with futuristic cities rising out of the desert sands.

Even before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran at the end of February, Vision 2030 was under strain, with speculation that some projects could be scrapped or dramatically scaled back as the plan's staggering ambition crashed into financial reality.

Now, amid unprecedented retaliatory attacks by Iran on its Gulf neighbours, including Saudi Arabia and massive disruption to global shipping routes due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, it's facing the perfect storm.

Neil Quilliam says the war in Iran has struck a blow to Saudi's grand ambitions. (Foreign Correspondent: Hamish Harty)

According to Dr Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow at Chatham House who specialises in global energy policy and Middle East politics, the war is directly affecting Saudi's ability to drum up funding.

"The vision is very much based on attracting foreign direct investment, so getting foreign companies to come and to commit to the country long-term. If there's instability in the region, then that's a great deterrence for international investors to come into the country," Dr Quilliam told Foreign Correspondent.

"Given that the country, number one, wants to attract and develop its tourist space, and number two, wants to be the host of international and regional events, instability is a drag on that."

Breaking Saudi's oil dependence

Vision 2030 is designed to help Saudi Arabia shift away from its dependence on oil to fill government coffers by transforming the country into an international investment, technology, tourism, sport and cultural powerhouse.

The Crown Prince, known as MBS, has his fingerprints all over the plan, as he seeks to reshape the country he will one day rule as king and prepare it to host one of the world's largest sporting festivals, the 2034 FIFA World Cup.

Much of the work is being steered by Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth vehicle, the Public Investment Fund (PIF), which itself is worth more than $1.5 trillion.

Mohammed bin Salman at the US–Saudi Investment Forum in Washington DC last year. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

In late 2025, Saudi Arabia's own budget reports showed more than half of the country's annual revenue came from the oil industry.

Since the Iran war broke out, Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure has come under Iranian attack, including the critical East–West oil pipeline, which enabled them to bypass Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz by piping oil west to ports on the Red Sea.

It's since been repaired, but Saudi has not been able to restore exports to pre-war volumes through its usual shipping lanes.

While surging oil prices are providing some relief to the budget bottom line, the supply chain interruption has only served to bolster MBS's thesis that the country needs to scale back its reliance on oil revenue.

Saudi Arabia has been ramping up its tourism industry to try to reduce economic dependence on oil revenue. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Davis)

But doing so has been more complicated than the Crown Prince initially bargained for.

Giga-plan visions in the desert

Some of Vision 2030's big-ticket items, often referred to as giga-projects, are massive city developments rising from the sands of the Saudi desert.

Perhaps the most ambitious and well-known example is NEOM, a region in the country's north-west, which was to include everything from luxury island resorts to a ski village.

Seen as MBS's signature project, its centrepiece was The Line, a surreal 170km-long linear city supposed to house 9 million people.

With an eye-watering reported initial price tag of $2.2 trillion and $80 billion already poured into NEOM, The Line has reportedly been scaled back to a far more modest proposition.

An artist's impression of part of The Line from above. (Supplied: NEOM)

Earlier this month, the governor of the PIF, Yasir Al-Rymayyan, insisted NEOM remained a key project.

"It is a major global economic zone," he said. "No project in NEOM has been cancelled. Has anything been postponed? Certainly, yes.

"Why? Some projects have been delayed because they are not on the critical path. There is no critical impact."

But despite that, the PIF has announced that spending as part of Vision 2030 was being cut back or reprioritised.

One area likely to be affected is the breakaway LIV Golf competition.

"The economy was already beginning to contract, young Saudis were always already beginning to sort of be laid off in the economy, so there had to be a recalibration, a refocus," said Dr Quilliam.

Funding for the LIV Golf breakaway tournament is among the Saudi initiatives now facing an uncertain future. (Foreign Correspondent: Matthew Doran)

"And then, obviously with the conflict, that's really kind of pushed the moment that they need to unveil the strategy — and it's all about showing business as usual."

Putting Saudi 'at the axis' of global sport

Before the war, Foreign Correspondent travelled to Saudi Arabia to witness the dramatic transformation taking shape.

One example of the country's jostling for global attention could be seen at a provincial football stadium in the city of Buraidah, 350km north-west of the capital, Riyadh.

More than 10,000 fans were waiting to watch a Friday night match between Saudi Pro league minnows Al Kholood and one of the competition's so-called "big four", Al Nassr, captained by football superstar Cristiano Ronaldo.

Cristiano Ronaldo takes the field for Saudi club Al Nassr in February this year. (Foreign Correspondent: Matthew Doran)

Young football fans at a match between Saudi clubs Al Kholood and Al Nassr. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Davis)

While he had spent most of his career playing in front of far larger crowds, the 40-year-old's tenure in the kingdom has cemented his status as the world's highest-paid athlete.

His last contract extension was reportedly worth more than $345 million per season and was said to include an equity stake in Al Nassr.

"I think people in the region, maybe, were following the clubs and the competition and some of the big players, but it wasn't at the tip of anyone's tongue, let's say, outside of the region," said Al Kholood's owner, Ben Harburg.

The American investor, originally from New Mexico, said that was now changing.

Ben Harburg (centre) says Saudi Arabia is becoming a global centre for sport. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Davis)

He was the first foreigner to own a Saudi football team after being invited by the PIF to buy Al Kholood and signing the deal for an undisclosed sum.

"I repeat this over and over, ad nauseam, but I don't think that football is a great investment, I think there are much easier, stress-free ways to make money," he said.

"But the reality is that the poles of global sport have shifted, and Saudi Arabia now very much sits at the axis of a lot of the things that are going on."

Expats from around the world are among those Vision 2030 is relying on to help guide the transformation.

Danny Townsend, the former chief of Australian football's A-Leagues, is now the chief executive of Saudi Arabia's SURJ Sports, the kingdom's sport-focused investment vehicle.

Danny Townsend is among the expats taking part in Saudi Arabia's transformation. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Davis)

"When you think about where the country's come from in the last 15 years, certainly we were a lot further behind a lot of our other Gulf neighbours," he said.

"And I think we've made a conscious effort to try to accelerate that growth in order to meet the market demand that is here.

"I think there's an impatience as well. The crown prince certainly has got a bold vision and he wants to achieve what he wants to achieve as quickly as he can."

Accusations of 'sportswashing'

The scale of the transformation in Saudi Arabia has its critics, with some accusing MBS of "sportswashing": using sports to distract from the country's record on human rights.

British journalist and author James Montague, who wrote the book Engulfed, examining the role of sport in the new Saudi Arabia, believes the term is too simplistic.

James Montague says the world has gotten over its qualms about the 2018 murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi. (Foreign Correspondent)

"What's going on here is something much more powerful, it's much more political, it's soft power," said Montague.

"It's using sport in a way that's not only to distract, it's to rebuild, and it's also about making yourself economically and culturally indispensable to the rest of the world."

Vision 2030 relies on more than just Saudi oil money, with the country seeking around $140 billion in foreign investment as part of the plans.

The 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in the country's embassy in Istanbul, which US intelligence said was ordered by MBS, spooked some investors.

Richard Branson was one of those who pulled out of deals in the kingdom in protest.

US intelligence agencies concluded Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi's murder was approved by MBS. (AP: Hasan Jamali, file)

"Ultimately, the murder of Jamal Khashoggi, as close as it came to ruining MBS's reputation — the world moved past it," said Montague.

"What I think MBS, and certainly his cadre of followers and people around him worked out, is that ultimately the West, they follow the money and they came back.

"It's almost difficult to imagine any single act that Saudi Arabia could do that could stop people wanting to make business with it, especially when you have Trump in the White House."

The 'worst-case scenario' for Saudi's grand vision

That theory is likely to be tested if hostilities between the US and Iran drag on and continue to involve the wider Gulf region.

Michael Ratney, the Biden administration's Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, believes the current war and the uncertainty about the future is the "worst-case scenario" for Saudi.

A US aircraft lies damaged on the runway in a strike at the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia during the Iran war in March. (Reuters)

"This is sort of the mother of all conflicts in the region — this is their major antagonist and adversary in a full-on war with the United States, and the Saudis and the Emiratis and everyone else in the Gulf is right in the middle of it," he said.

Mr Ratney, who has not been replaced in Riyadh by the Trump White House, has argued the Saudis have "no love for the Iranian regime."

"They would love to see them dispatched. On the other hand, I think they're pretty sober about the ability of the US or Israel to do that," he said.

"And I think they're worried about being stuck with the results of an inconclusive war, especially if Iran retains control of the Strait of Hormuz."

Construction underway at Quiddiyah, a planned city outside Riyadh. (Foreign Correspondent: Matthew Doran)

A roller-coaster built by American theme park giant Six Flags at Quiddiya reaches speeds of 250km/h. (Foreign Correspondent: Matthew Doran)

Saudi Arabia host US forces and the country's embassy in Riyadh has been targeted by a drone attack.

There has been debate as to whether the war, and specifically Iran's attacks, would prompt some regional allies to reconsider their ties with the United States.

"That's unknowable until the dust settles, until the war is over and they and we and others in the region have had an opportunity to think this through," said Ratney.

"It's easy to say, 'Oh, they're disappointed in the United States, they're going to look for partnerships elsewhere.'

"On the other hand, they have a lot invested in the relationship with the US.

"It may well be that they decide that the US is going to continue to be their partner, they would like greater clarity about the relationship, but meanwhile, they hedge and they pursue deeper partnerships with others at the same time."

Watch Saudi's Reality Check tonight on Foreign Correspondent at 8pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: Penny Wong confronts the limits of Australia's China strategy
World.content:
When Foreign Minister Penny Wong travels to Japan, China and South Korea this week, she will move through a region where relationships point in different directions at the same time.

On the surface, the alignment is familiar. China is Australia's largest trading partner but also its most complex strategic challenge. Japan is a close security partner. South Korea sits between them, tied to both Washington and Beijing in different ways.

But that surface hides a more intricate reality. The ties between China, Japan and South Korea are not linear. They are layered, shaped by history, domestic politics and shifting strategic incentives.

Understanding those layers is central to understanding the diplomatic terrain Wong faces.

China's relationship with each of its neighbours follows a distinct pattern.

With Japan, the relationship is structurally tense. It combines deep economic interdependence with persistent political distrust. Even when leaders attempt to stabilise ties, progress is fragile and easily reversed.

With South Korea, the relationship is more flexible. There is no equivalent historical burden, and both sides have strong incentives to cooperate — trade, regional stability and the management of North Korea. But that flexibility has limits.

With Australia, the relationship is different again. There is no deep historical hostility. Tensions have been driven primarily by contemporary strategic and political disagreements. That has allowed for a partial reset, but not a full resolution.

For Wong, this means dealing with three versions of China at once: defensive and sensitive with Japan, pragmatic but conditional with South Korea, and selectively stabilising with Australia.

China's relationship with each of its neighbours follows a distinct pattern. With Japan, the relationship is structurally tense. (Reuters: Kim Kyung-Hoon)

The most fragile line

Among these relationships, the China-Japan axis is the most volatile.

Australia's ties with Japan are deep and expanding, particularly in defence and security.

For Canberra, this is a response to a more uncertain regional environment. For Beijing, those same moves are viewed through a different lens.

China's distrust of Japan is not only strategic. It is also shaped by the unresolved legacy of Japan's wartime actions in China.

That history is consistently reinforced in public messaging and education, and it continues to influence how Chinese officials and the public interpret Japan's role in the region.

This has practical consequences for Australia.

Closer cooperation with Japan, whether through joint exercises, defence agreements or regional initiatives, can be seen in Beijing as part of a broader effort to limit China's influence.

That perception does not depend on Australia's stated intent.

For Wong, the challenge is to maintain and deepen Australia's partnership with Japan while managing the way those actions are read in Beijing.

That requires careful signalling, particularly at a time when military activity in the region is increasing and the risk of miscalculation remains present.

A more adaptable relationship

China's relationship with South Korea presents a different set of considerations for Australia.

Japan deploys first long range missile as tensions with China esculate The country is pushing to bolster its offensive capabilities since tensions with China have escalated over Taiwan.

Unlike its ties with Japan, Beijing's relationship with Seoul is more adaptable. The two countries have strong economic links, and China sees South Korea as relevant to managing North Korea.

At the same time, the relationship has defined limits.

When South Korea deployed a US missile defence system, China responded with a range of economic measures that affected tourism, retail and cultural exports. The episode demonstrated Beijing's willingness to use economic leverage in response to security decisions it opposes.

That experience continues to shape South Korea's approach. Seoul engages with China, but it does so with caution and a clear awareness of the potential costs.

For Australia, this has two implications.

It shows how China may respond when it sees its security interests challenged. This is something Canberra has already experienced in a different context.

It also highlights that regional partners do not all take the same approach to China.

Even countries aligned with the US will adjust their positions when economic pressure is applied.

Wong's engagement with Seoul therefore needs to account for that difference. Policy alignment cannot be assumed, particularly on issues involving China.

Beijing's external behaviour reflects both strategic ambition and domestic constraint. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

An assertive China

Beijing's external behaviour reflects both strategic ambition and domestic constraint.

Its more assertive diplomatic style in recent years has been widely noted.

The direct tone, often described as "wolf-warrior diplomacy", signals a shift in how Beijing wants to be treated — not as a rising power seeking accommodation, but as one demanding recognition.

At the same time, this posture is shaped by internal expectations. Public opinion has been influenced by decades of messaging about national strength, sovereignty and historical grievance.

That has created an environment where compromise on sensitive issues can be interpreted as weakness.

For the government, this narrows the space for manoeuvre. It must project firmness, even when it is pursuing stability.

This dual dynamic — outward confidence, inward constraint — explains why China's diplomacy can appear inconsistent.

To understand that calibration, it is necessary to look at how China remembers its past.

The country's modern history includes periods of foreign domination, war and internal upheaval.

Commemorative events and official narratives emphasise national suffering and recovery. This framing reinforces a sense of vigilance and the need to guard against external pressure.

The effect is cumulative. It shapes public expectations and influences how international events are interpreted.

It also helps explain the persistence of strong leadership models in Chinese politics.

A government seen as defending national interests is more likely to maintain legitimacy than one perceived as conceding ground.

Loading

The competing pressures for Canberra

For Australia, these dynamics come together in a particularly exposed way.

The recent stabilisation in Australia-China relations has reopened channels of dialogue and eased trade disruptions. But it has not removed the underlying strategic tension of keeping a balance between Beijing and Washington.

Domestic politics adds to the challenge. Public debate in Australia often frames Beijing in negative terms, while economic realities demand ongoing positive engagement.

For Wong, the task is to manage this contradiction. She needs to maintain a working relationship with Beijing without undermining Australia's broader strategic posture.

Her visit also takes place against a broader regional backdrop.

Japan is reassessing its security role in response to a more uncertain international environment.

South Korea is expanding its global influence, including through culture and technology.

China is seeking to shape the regional order in ways that reflect its growing power.

At the same time, confidence in the US as a consistent strategic anchor has been tested, prompting allies to rethink their options.

This has created a more fluid, and more uncertain, environment, where diplomacy is less about resolution than about management.

Wong's trip will not settle the tensions between China and Japan, nor will it resolve the strategic dilemmas facing South Korea. It will not eliminate the structural pressures shaping China's behaviour.

What it can do is help navigate them. It requires recognising that relationships in Northeast Asia are not binary. They are complex and often contradictory.

For a foreign minister, the challenge is to work within it.

World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America Shooting suspect charged with attempting to assassinate Trump Michael Koziol Updated April 28, 2026 — 5:52am ,first published 4:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Washington: Alleged Washington hotel shooter Cole Tomas Allen faces a maximum sentence of life in prison after he was charged with attempting to assassinate the president of the United States. Allen, 31, appeared in court for the first time on Monday afternoon (US time) wearing a short-sleeve light blue prison uniform. US President Donald Trump shared a photo of the alleged gunman. Truth Social/@realDonaldTrump He appeared calm as judge Matthew Sharbaugh explained his legal rights, and he affirmed that he understood. He did not ask any questions of the judge. Three US court marshalls surrounded the defence bench. Allen glanced at the packed courtroom gallery several times, and mostly kept his eyes on whomever was speaking. At the hearing’s conclusion, he was led out of the courtroom without handcuffs.



In addition to the attempted assassination charge, Allen was also charged with transporting a firearm across state lines with intent to commit a felony, and discharging a firearm in a crime of violence. Those offences carry potential jail terms, with the latter a mandatory minimum 10-year sentence. Allen will remain in police custody until at least Thursday, when he will appear before a bail hearing. Both parties also agreed to a preliminary case hearing on May 11. Federal prosecutor Jocelyn Ballantine said the government alleged that Allen “attempted to assassinate the president of the United States with a 12-gauge pump action shotgun”. He was also allegedly found with a handgun and three knives, prosecutors told the court. Allen’s court-appointed lawyers noted he had no prior convictions and was presumed innocent until proven guilty.



The US attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, was seated in the courtroom’s front row for the 10-minute hearing. Related Article Donald Trump Inside the pandemonium at the Washington Hilton At a later press conference, Pirro and other US officials confirmed key details of the government’s case against Allen, and said additional charges would be laid. “Make no mistake – this was an attempted assassination of the president of the United States, with the defendant making clear what his intent was,” Pirro said. “That intent was to bring down as many of the high-ranking cabinet officials as he could. This is the kind of situation that we cannot tolerate.”



The prosecution alleges that on April 6, Allen booked a three-night stay at the Washington Hilton from April 24 to 27. On April 21, he left his home near Los Angeles and travelled by train to Chicago, before arriving in Washington on April 24. He allegedly wrote a manifesto that he sent to family members minutes before the attack. Pirro said his writings may appear a bit “la la la”, but his intention to target Trump administration officials was clear. “Any suggestion that he wasn’t there to do harm is absurd.” Allen was not charged with assaulting a federal officer on Monday, as Pirro had previously indicated he would be. Acting US attorney-general Todd Blanche said it had not been confirmed whose bullet struck the Secret Service agent who was injured in the attack. “We want to get that right. We’re still looking at that,” Blanche said. “All the evidence is being examined very carefully and expeditiously, and we’ll know more soon. “We do believe ... defendant fired out of his shotgun. But as far as getting into exact ballistics, I’m not going to do that today.”

World.title: ASX set to fall, Wall Street steady as oil prices rise; Microsoft, OpenAI loosen partnership
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to fall, Wall Street steady as oil prices rise; Microsoft, OpenAI loosen partnership Stan Choe April 28, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The US stock market’s record-breaking rally is stalling after uncertainty rose over the weekend about what will happen next in the Iran war, while oil prices rose. The S&P 500 rose 0.1 per cent, coming off its latest all-time high driven by strong profit reports from US companies and hopes that the global economy can avoid a worst-case scenario because of the war. The Dow Jones was down 80 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq rose 0.1 per cent above its own record. Wall Street is treading water on Monday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 4.55am AEST pointing to a fall of 56 points, or 0.6 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.2 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar is 0.5 per cent higher at US71.48¢. The moves were stronger in the oil market, where prices climbed roughly 3 per cent as tankers still find the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed. That’s keeping crude stuck in the Middle East and away from customers worldwide, including oil produced by Iran that’s being blockaded by the US Navy.



Iran has offered to reopen the strait if the United States ends its blockade, while proposing that discussions on the larger question of its nuclear program would come in a later phase. But US President Donald Trump seems unlikely to accept the offer, which was passed to the Americans by Pakistan. Over the weekend, Trump told US envoys not to go to Pakistan, which has been playing a crucial mediating role. By saying the Iranians could call Washington with any proposal, Trump appeared to signal he’s content to try to continue to squeeze Iran with the blockade. Related Article Middle East at war ‘Basically sending someone unarmed into war’: The life-or-death decision Silke faces every day The price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in June climbed 3.2 per cent to $US108.73. Brent to be delivered in July, which is where more of the trading is happening in the oil market, rose 2.9 per cent to $US101.99 per barrel. Brent prices were at only about $US70 per barrel before the war and have briefly shot to nearly $US120 a couple of times when fears about the war have hit their heights.



Most big US companies have nevertheless been reporting profits for the start of 2026 that have topped analysts’ expectations. That’s helped the S&P 500 jump nearly 13 per cent since hitting a low in late March. Verizon Communications joined the list, and its stock climbed 3 per cent after the company said it added more postpaid phone customers than it lost during a first quarter for the first time since 2013. It also raised its forecast for profit growth this year, even though its revenue for the first quarter fell short of analysts’ expectations. Domino’s Pizza helped drag on the market and fell 9.5 per cent after it reported weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Several of Wall Street’s most influential stocks are scheduled to deliver their own profit reports this week, including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Microsoft all on Wednesday. Apple will report on Thursday. Overnight, it was announced Microsoft is losing exclusive access to OpenAI’s technology, clearing the way for the ChatGPT creator to sell its products across rival cloud platforms in a sweeping change to one of the artificial intelligence era’s most consequential alliances. The reworked tie-up, announced jointly by the companies on Monday, retains Microsoft as OpenAI’s primary cloud partner with a license to the startup’s intellectual property through 2032. It also paves the way for OpenAI to take its models to Amazon.com’s cloud unit, without any technical workarounds.



In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher with the rise in oil prices. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note rose to 4.34 per cent from 4.31 per cent late Friday. Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war Putin’s pain: The walls are closing in on Russia Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The Federal Reserve will announce its latest move on interest rates on Wednesday, and the consensus expectation among traders is that it will hold rates steady. Lower rates would give the economy a boost, but they would also threaten to worsen inflation when oil prices are in flux and tariffs are also threatening to raise prices for all kinds of products. Wednesday will likely be the final meeting where Chair Jerome Powell will lead the Fed. His term as chair is scheduled to expire next month, and Trump has already named a nominee for his replacement, Kevin Warsh. The European Central Bank, Bank of Japan and Bank of England will also be announcing their own interest-rate decisions this week.



In stock markets abroad, indexes slipped in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2.2 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.4 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. AP with Reuters The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
